days.title: Cloud Benefits, Agentic AI, and Digital Transformation

concepts.heading: What Cloud and Infrastructure Mean
concepts.body: Cloud computing is the on-demand availability of computing resources, such as storage and processing power, delivered as services over the internet. The customer does not buy and look after physical servers, the room, the power and the cooling. A provider owns and runs them, and the customer rents what it needs and pays for what it uses. Infrastructure is the foundation that applications and data depend on: compute (servers and virtual machines), storage and networking, plus the facilities that house them. On premises, a company buys and operates all of this itself. In the cloud, the provider supplies it as a service. When a leader says the company will modernize its infrastructure, that means using those resources more effectively, for example with containers or serverless computing, or by taking advantage of a cloud provider's global network. A useful memory aid is three words: on demand, as a service, pay for use. A small software team that needs a test environment this afternoon and will switch it off on Friday is using the cloud model. A team that must order servers and wait for delivery is not.

concepts.heading: The Benefits of Cloud
concepts.body: The exam expects you to match a business pain to the cloud benefit that answers it. Scalability: capacity rises and falls with demand, so a company stops buying for the busiest week of the year. Cost-effectiveness: spending follows usage, and nobody pays to house, power and maintain idle hardware (cloud is still not free, so costs must be managed). Agility and speed: resources appear on demand, so a pilot can start in days instead of waiting months for procurement and can be dropped cheaply if it fails. Flexibility: services can be reached from anywhere with an internet connection and resized as needs change. Global reach and high availability: services can run near users in many places and survive the loss of one site. Security: large providers invest in security mechanisms and expert teams that most companies cannot match alone. Data-driven insights: data held in one platform is easier to analyze. Strategic focus: staff move from patching servers to building features that set the company apart. Example: a streaming company entering new countries wants fast playback everywhere, which is global reach.

concepts.heading: Digital Transformation: Drivers, Challenges, and the Cost of Standing Still
concepts.body: Digital transformation means using modern digital technologies, including public, private and hybrid cloud, to create or change business processes, culture and customer experiences so the company can meet changing market conditions. It is more than a technology move: shifting servers to a provider without changing how the business works is a migration, not yet a transformation. Common drivers are changing customer expectations, competitive pressure from rivals that use cloud and AI to launch faster, large volumes of data that need analysis, pressure to cut cost, and the wish to break down silos between teams. The challenges are usually human rather than technical: resistance to change, skills gaps, siloed data and teams, legacy systems and processes, and weak commitment from business and IT leaders. A company that buys an excellent platform but keeps manual approvals and separate spreadsheets has a culture and process problem. Not adopting cloud is also a decision with a risk: slowly falling behind competitors, paying for hardware that is idle or too small, and missing new capabilities that arrive first as cloud services.

concepts.heading: Agentic AI
concepts.body: Generative AI creates new content, such as text, images or code, from a prompt. Agentic AI goes further. It uses a large language model as the brain of agents that pursue a goal by using tools: the agent perceives information from data sources and systems, reasons about what to do, plans the steps, acts in other systems and reflects on the result to adjust next time. Google describes agentic AI as a subset of generative AI that goes beyond content creation and simple function calling. An AI agent is a building block that handles a specific task, while agentic AI is the coordinated use of agents to run a wider workflow. Example: a generative tool can draft a marketing email, but an agentic system could also schedule the campaign, watch the results and change the next message. Business uses include customer service, supply chain management, healthcare, financial services and software development. A fixed FAQ bot that matches keywords or a tool that only forwards a ticket to a person does not reason, plan or act, so it is not agentic. Google stresses clear objectives, good data and human oversight.

concepts.heading: What Sets Google Cloud Apart
concepts.body: The guide groups Google Cloud's differentiators into a few ideas. Openness and interoperability: Google Cloud supports multicloud and hybrid setups and builds on open source, with Kubernetes (which began at Google and powers Google Kubernetes Engine) as the best-known example. Open source code is public to view, change and share; an open standard is a published specification anyone can implement. Both reduce vendor lock-in. An AI-ready data platform: BigQuery for data, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform for ML development and AI accelerators come together, so a company can build AI on its own data without moving it between disconnected tools. AI Hypercomputer is Google's integrated system for AI workloads, combining TPUs and GPUs, open software and flexible consumption options, which gives hardware choice and cost control. Security: capabilities built secure by design and by default, informed by frontline intelligence. Global network: one of the largest networks in the world, connecting over 200 countries and territories, with edge locations near users to lower latency. Example: a bank training models on its own transaction data wants the data and ML tools in one place.

examPoints: Match the pain to the benefit: idle peak capacity is scalability, months of procurement is agility and speed, fixed servers to patch is strategic focus, users on many continents is global reach and high availability.

Digital transformation changes processes, culture and customer experience, so the hurdles are mainly people and process (resistance, skills gaps, silos), and not adopting cloud carries the risk of falling behind.

Agentic AI perceives, reasons, plans, acts and reflects using tools, whereas generative AI creates content; Google Cloud differentiators include openness (Kubernetes, open standards), an AI-ready data platform, AI Hypercomputer, security and the global network.

quiz.q: An airline is evaluating a new system. It reads delay data from operations feeds, works out which passengers need new itineraries, rebooks them through the reservation system and then reviews how well the plan worked so it can improve the next one. Which description fits this system?
choices: A data warehouse, because it collects operational data from many sources into one place for analysis
Agentic AI, because it perceives data, plans steps, acts in other systems and reflects on the results
Generative AI only, because its main job is to produce a written apology message for each passenger
A business intelligence dashboard, because it reports on past flight delays for managers to read
quiz.explain: The system pursues a goal, acts in other systems and learns from the outcome, which is the agentic loop. The warehouse in option A stores data for analysis and neither plans nor acts. The dashboard only reports on the past and is not agentic either.

quiz.q: After moving its applications to a cloud provider, a company's CEO announces, 'The provider now handles all security, including who is allowed to see our customer data.' How should a Cloud Digital Leader respond?
choices: Cloud providers do secure the underlying infrastructure, but the company is still responsible for its own data, user access and how it configures services
The CEO is correct, because moving to the cloud transfers every security duty to the provider, including decisions about who may see customer data
The CEO is incorrect, because cloud is less secure than a company's own data center and the company should move its customer data back on premises
The CEO is correct, because identities and data are protected automatically once the contract with the provider is signed and nothing more is needed
quiz.explain: Cloud security is shared: the provider protects the infrastructure, while the customer decides who can access data and how services are set up. Choice D sounds reassuring but no contract removes the customer's duty for identities and data. Large providers are generally recognized as offering strong security, so avoiding the cloud for that reason is not supported.

days.recap: Cloud is on-demand, pay-for-use computing; match each business pain to a benefit (scalability, cost, agility, flexibility, global reach, security, insights, focus). Transformation changes process and culture, agentic AI acts through tools, and Google Cloud stands out through openness, AI-ready data, AI Hypercomputer, security and its network.

days.title: Private, Hybrid, and Multicloud, Networking, and Google Locations

concepts.heading: Public, Private, and Hybrid Cloud
concepts.body: Three architecture terms describe where workloads run. A public cloud is infrastructure and services run by a provider such as Google Cloud and shared by many customers. A private cloud is cloud-style infrastructure used by a single organization, usually in its own data center. It gives the most control over placement, configuration and physical access, which suits strict control or compliance needs, but the organization buys, houses and maintains the hardware and must add capacity before demand arrives. A hybrid cloud connects private or on-premises environments with a public cloud so that applications and data work across both. Companies choose hybrid when some rules say certain data must stay in a place they control, when they want to modernize step by step instead of moving everything at once, or when some systems cannot move yet. Example: a regional bank must keep account records in its own data center under data residency rules, but wants public cloud analytics and elastic capacity for new customer apps. Two environments working together is the definition of hybrid, so neither private only nor public only fits.

concepts.heading: Multicloud and Its Trade-Off
concepts.body: Multicloud means using services from more than one public cloud provider, often choosing a provider per workload. The documented benefits are best of each cloud (match each workload to the provider whose features suit it), less vendor lock-in, access to innovation from any provider, and redundancy so a problem at one provider need not stop everything. The cost is complexity: providers differ in features, tools, APIs and service agreements, so teams need a consistent way to manage, secure and monitor workloads everywhere. Good multicloud management means one view of workloads, the same security and compliance policies applied everywhere, and monitoring that shows end-to-end health. Hybrid and multicloud are often confused. Hybrid combines private or on-premises with public. Multicloud needs at least two public providers. A company with its own data center plus one public cloud is hybrid, not multicloud. A hybrid setup can also be multicloud if it includes two public providers, but it is not automatically so. Google Cloud supports both, building on open source such as Kubernetes to keep applications portable (GKE Enterprise manages Kubernetes across such environments).

concepts.heading: Networking Basics for Business Conversations
concepts.body: Four terms come up repeatedly. An IP address is a numeric label that identifies a device or service on a network, like a street address for data packets. A domain name is the readable name people type, such as a company website address. DNS, the Domain Name System, translates domain names into IP addresses so the browser knows where to connect. A company can move its site to a new IP address during a cloud migration and update DNS while the name customers use stays the same, and if DNS fails customers cannot find the site even though the servers are fine. Latency is the delay before data arrives, usually measured in milliseconds, and it grows with distance. Real-time uses such as video calls, gaming and trading are sensitive to it. Bandwidth is how much data a connection can carry in a given time, which limits things like moving large backups. Highway analogy: latency is how long one car takes to drive from A to B, and bandwidth is how many lanes there are. A lag in a live class is latency, and slow upload of big files is bandwidth.

concepts.heading: Regions, Zones, and Edge Locations
concepts.body: Google Cloud's physical footprint has layers. A region is a specific geographic area where Google Cloud has resources. A region contains multiple zones. A zone is a deployment area inside a region and acts as a separate failure domain: a power or cooling problem in one zone should not affect the others, and zones in a region are linked by fast, low-latency connections. An edge location is a network point of presence close to end users, used to deliver content and traffic quickly. Each layer solves a different business problem. Zones give resilience: spread an application across multiple zones in one region and it keeps running if one zone fails, which is the lowest-effort way to gain high availability. Multiple regions protect against the loss of a whole region but cost more effort and money. Regions also give placement choice. Pick a region by latency to users, data residency and compliance, availability of the services you need, and price and sustainability. Example: an insurer serving customers in Germany and France chooses a European region so claims data stays where rules require and responses are quick.

concepts.heading: Google's Global Network and Digital Transformation
concepts.body: Google Cloud runs on the same global network that Google uses for its own services. It connects over 200 countries and territories with terrestrial and subsea fiber, and includes edge locations close to users. Google describes the network as minimizing latency and security risks for enterprise applications and AI training. Two ideas matter. First, a private backbone: traffic that enters Google's network travels on Google-managed infrastructure for much of its journey instead of crossing a patchwork of public internet networks, which makes performance more predictable. Second, proximity: edge locations serve content and some workloads near users, so data travels a shorter distance. For a business, this means lower and more consistent latency, better customer experience, and the ability to serve new markets without building its own network. Distance cannot be removed entirely, so if idle servers sit in North America but customers in Southeast Asia complain about slow pages, the fix is to bring the application closer, with a nearby region or edge locations, not to buy more server capacity. This ties directly to the digital transformation goal of reaching customers anywhere.

examPoints: Hybrid combines private or on-premises with public cloud and suits residency rules and gradual modernization; multicloud needs two or more public providers and trades flexibility for management complexity.
IP address is the numeric label, DNS translates names into addresses, latency is delay and grows with distance, and bandwidth is capacity over time.

Zones are failure domains inside a region (use multiple zones for high availability), regions are chosen by latency, residency and service availability, and edge locations bring content close to users.

quiz.q: A news website stores its articles and photos on servers that are lightly loaded. Readers on another continent still wait a long time for photos to appear. Which Google Cloud concept most directly addresses this?
choices: Adding more servers in the original location, because slow photos always mean the servers are short of capacity for the readers' requests
Switching to a private cloud, because private infrastructure removes the effect of distance on how fast content is delivered to readers
Changing the website's domain name, because a shorter name lets browsers fetch the photos faster from the same distant servers
Edge locations, which serve content from points of presence close to the readers and shorten the distance data travels
quiz.explain: The servers are lightly loaded, so capacity is not the cause. Distance causes latency, and edge locations and nearby regions reduce it. Extra servers in the same place do not shorten the path. A private cloud and the length of a domain name have no effect on distance.

quiz.q: A hospital group must keep its regulated medical image archive in its own data center, but wants to start building AI features in a public cloud and move other systems over gradually. Which approach and benefit fit best?
choices: Multicloud, because it means keeping regulated data in a data center while using one public provider for the new AI features
Private cloud only, because it gives the hospital group public cloud AI services inside its own data center without any connection to a provider
Hybrid cloud, because it connects the private archive with public cloud services and lets the group modernize at its own pace
Public cloud only, because moving everything at once is the only way to use public cloud AI services and keep the archive compliant
quiz.explain: Hybrid combines private or on-premises infrastructure with a public cloud, which meets the residency rule and allows gradual migration. Choice A is tempting because many people use multicloud loosely, but multicloud means more than one public provider, not on-premises plus one provider.

days.recap: Private cloud gives control but you run the hardware, hybrid links private and public, and multicloud uses several public providers at the cost of complexity. Know IP, DNS, latency and bandwidth; zones give resilience, regions give placement, edge brings content close, and Google's global network supports all of it.

days.title: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, Shared Responsibility, and Domain 1 Review

concepts.heading: The Three Service Models
concepts.body: The service models differ in how much the provider manages and how much you manage. With Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) the provider supplies compute, storage and networking, and you manage the operating system, middleware, applications and data. Compute Engine virtual machines are the example. You get the most control and the most responsibility. With Platform as a Service (PaaS) the provider also manages the runtime environment and scaling, so you bring code and data. Cloud Run and App Engine are examples. You do less operational work and accept less control. With Software as a Service (SaaS) the provider delivers a complete application, managed and updated by the provider, and users simply use it, often in a browser. Google Workspace is the example. A way to remember the ladder: IaaS rents the machine, PaaS rents the place to run your code, SaaS rents the finished product. Models are not exclusive, and most companies use all three together with traditional IT. Example: a retailer runs its custom checkout code on PaaS, uses a standard collaboration suite as SaaS, and keeps a legacy inventory system on virtual machines it controls, which is IaaS.

concepts.heading: Choosing a Model: Benefits and Trade-Offs
concepts.body: Choose the model by asking how much control you need and how much operations work you want to avoid. IaaS fits workloads that need a specific operating system version, drivers or full control of the environment, such as a legacy application you want to move without changing. The benefit is hardware removed from your plate; the trade-off is that you still patch and secure the operating system. PaaS fits teams that want to write and deploy code quickly without server upkeep. Benefits are faster development, no server or OS maintenance and built-in scalability. Trade-offs are less control over the environment, limited customization and possible lock-in to the platform. SaaS fits standard needs such as email, calendars and document collaboration, especially for a small firm with no IT staff. Benefits are easy setup and access from any device. Limits are little control over infrastructure and security settings, little customization and possible difficulty integrating with existing tools. No model is better in general: the right answer is the one that matches the stated need. An on-premises private cloud, by contrast, leaves the company running its own hardware.

concepts.heading: Shared Responsibility at Concept Level
concepts.body: Security and operations in the cloud are shared between provider and customer, and the dividing line depends on the service model. The provider always secures the physical data centers, hardware and the underlying network. Beyond that, the more abstract the service, the more the provider takes on. In IaaS, the customer manages the operating system, middleware, applications and data, including patching and security configuration, so an unpatched operating system on a rented virtual machine is the customer's gap. In PaaS, the provider also manages the operating system and runtime, and the customer is responsible for application code and data. In SaaS, the provider manages almost everything, but the customer still owns its data and decides who can access it. The split is by layer of the stack, not by a share of servers. Two misunderstandings are common. First, thinking the provider handles everything once you move to cloud. Second, thinking nobody is responsible. Neither is true. Example: after an incident at a company renting virtual machines, the investigation points to missing operating system updates, which sit on the customer side of the line.

concepts.heading: Domain 1 Consolidation: Matching Needs to Concepts
concepts.body: Domain 1 questions describe a business situation and ask for the benefit, term or model that fits. A practical approach is to find the signal words. Idle servers outside the busy season and months waiting for hardware point to scalability and agility. A request for a memorable name instead of a number points to DNS. Complaints from one distant geography with idle servers point to latency, fixed by region or edge placement. A rule that data must stay in the company's data center while new apps use public services points to hybrid cloud, and wanting the best analytics from one provider and a platform from another points to multicloud and its management complexity. A need to run on a specific operating system points to IaaS, to run custom code without servers points to PaaS, and a standard application run by someone else is SaaS. A company that has the tools but keeps old habits has a culture, skills or leadership hurdle, not a technology one. Finally, avoid vendor lock-in with openness: open source for code, open standards for interfaces, and Kubernetes as the portable foundation Google Cloud highlights.

concepts.heading: Common Traps in Domain 1
concepts.body: Several wrong answers recur. Cloud is not free: pay-for-use means costs follow consumption and still need management. Multicloud is not simply any mix of environments: it requires more than one public provider. Moving servers is not digital transformation by itself, since the definition includes processes, culture and customer experience. Regions are not the same as zones: a zone is a failure domain inside a region, and spreading over zones protects against a zone problem while multiple regions protect against a regional one at greater effort and cost. Latency and bandwidth are different measures, delay versus capacity. Open source is about available code and open standards about published specifications. Agentic AI acts through tools, while generative AI creates content. Shared responsibility never moves your data and user access decisions to the provider, even in SaaS. When two options look similar, check which exact term the scenario describes. Example: a CIO who says the company is already multicloud because it has a data center and one public cloud is describing a hybrid setup, and the fix is to name it correctly, not to claim extra benefits.

examPoints: IaaS gives the most control and responsibility (you manage the OS), PaaS runs your code on a platform the provider manages, and SaaS is a finished application with the least control and effort.
Shared responsibility is split by layer of the stack: the provider secures the infrastructure, and the customer always remains responsible for its data and for who can access it.
Pick the answer that matches the exact term in the scenario: hybrid is not multicloud, a zone is not a region, latency is not bandwidth, and moving servers is not by itself transformation.

quiz.q: A city government wants its own developers to build and launch a resident complaint portal quickly. The city does not want its staff to patch operating systems or size servers, and it accepts having less control over the environment. Which service model fits?
choices: Infrastructure as a Service, because the provider also patches the operating system on every rented virtual machine
Software as a Service, because the city can write its own application code inside any finished product
Platform as a Service, because the provider runs the infrastructure and runtime while the city supplies code and data
A private cloud, because the city's own staff would then be free of all server maintenance
quiz.explain: PaaS matches a team that wants to focus on code. The IaaS choice is wrong because in IaaS the customer manages and patches the operating system. SaaS provides a finished application and is not a place to deploy custom code. A private cloud leaves the city operating the hardware.

quiz.q: A professional-services firm switches its customer relationship management to a Software as a Service product. Which statement about responsibility is accurate?
choices: The firm is responsible for patching the operating system underneath the application, because SaaS customers manage the servers and the platform
The provider runs the application and infrastructure, but the firm remains responsible for its data and for deciding who can access it
The provider is responsible for everything including which employees may view customer records, so the firm has no remaining duties at all
Responsibility is split by percentage of servers used, so the firm owns half of the infrastructure risk and the provider owns the other half
quiz.explain: Even with SaaS the customer keeps ownership of its data and access decisions. Claiming the firm patches the operating system gets it backwards, because the provider manages that layer in SaaS. Saying the provider decides who may view records ignores the customer's access duty, and responsibility is divided by layer of the stack, not by a share of servers.

days.recap: IaaS rents the machine, PaaS rents the platform for your code, SaaS rents the finished app; control and responsibility shrink as you climb. The provider secures infrastructure, you always own your data and access. In Domain 1, match the exact term in the scenario and avoid mixing hybrid with multicloud or zones with regions.

days.title: Why Data Matters: Stores, Data Types, Supply Chain, and Governance

concepts.heading: Why Data Is Valuable
concepts.body: Data alone is just stored records. It becomes valuable when it changes what people decide or do. The exam guide lists several ways data creates value: generating real-time business insights, identifying trends, informing strategic decision making and fueling AI. Real-time insight means events such as a sale or stock movement are analyzed as they arrive, so someone can act the same day instead of reading a report about last quarter. Trends and strategic decisions come from combining data across many periods and sources, which shows patterns no single person sees and lets leaders back major choices with evidence instead of instinct alone. Data also fuels AI: models learn patterns from data and, in generative and agentic applications, are grounded in the organization's own records. If those records are scattered, stale or inconsistent, the AI inherits those problems. Example: an insurer is disappointed by a vague AI claims assistant, and the cause is poorly organized claims data, not the AI tool. The leadership takeaway is that AI projects are data projects first, and relevant, current, trustworthy data beats simply having more data.

concepts.heading: Database, Data Warehouse, and Data Lake
concepts.body: These three stores serve different jobs. A database stores the data an application needs to run. It handles many small reads and writes, such as recording a single money transfer, and keeps each record accurate at that moment. This is called operational or transactional work. A data warehouse is an enterprise platform for analysis and reporting, from sources such as point-of-sale, marketing and CRM systems. It keeps current and historical data together for a long-range view, and BigQuery is Google Cloud's serverless data warehouse. A data lake is a centralized repository that holds large amounts of structured, semi-structured and unstructured data in its native format without a predefined schema. It keeps full-fidelity original data, which suits exploration and machine learning when questions are not yet known, and Cloud Storage commonly serves as its storage layer. Companies use all three, keeping databases apart from the warehouse because heavy reporting queries over years of data would compete with the quick updates customers are waiting for. Google also describes an open lakehouse that combines warehouse-style performance with lake flexibility.

concepts.heading: Types of Data: By Source and by Shape
concepts.body: Data is classified two ways. By source, relative to the organization. First-party data is collected directly by the organization from its own customers and channels, such as purchases, website behavior and loyalty sign-ups. It is usually the most relevant and trusted. Second-party data is another organization's first-party data that it shares directly with you, usually under an agreement, such as an airline sharing anonymized booking data with a hotel group. Third-party data is collected by an outside party with no direct relationship to your customers and sold or licensed broadly, such as an aggregator's audience list. It can add reach, but quality, freshness and consent are harder to check, and competitors can buy the same lists. By shape. Structured data fits a fixed schema of rows and columns, like a transaction table. Semi-structured data has tags or keys that organize it but no rigid table schema, such as JSON or XML messages. Unstructured data has no predefined model, such as free text, images, audio and video. These are generally accepted definitions, not Google Cloud product terms. Do not confuse unlabeled with unstructured: unlabeled is a machine learning term.

concepts.heading: The Data Supply Chain
concepts.body: The data supply chain follows data from creation to business use in six stages. Genesis: data is created by an event, such as a card tap, a purchase or a sensor reading. Collection: data is gathered and brought in from its sources, through streams or batch loads. Processing: data is cleaned, validated, de-duplicated and transformed so it is usable, and on Google Cloud services such as Dataflow and Managed Service for Apache Spark do this kind of work. Storage: data is kept in a suitable system, such as a database, warehouse or lake. Analysis: data is examined for patterns, answers and predictions, for example in BigQuery or a Looker dashboard. Activation: results are used to take action, such as personalizing an offer or showing an agent a retention suggestion during a call. These are generally accepted stage names, not product names. A quick test for any activity is to ask whether it creates, moves, fixes, keeps, studies or uses the data. Many organizations stop after analysis and produce reports nobody uses, and activation closes the loop. Example: dashboards that show inflated production counts because duplicate sensor readings were never removed point to a missing processing step.

concepts.heading: Governance, Silos, and Openness
concepts.body: Data governance is everything an organization does to make data secure, private, accurate, available and usable for analysis, machine learning and building agents. It means setting internal standards for how data is gathered and processed, naming owners, agreeing shared definitions and defining who may access sensitive information. It addresses inconsistent numbers, unclear access, compliance gaps (for example GDPR or CCPA) and silos. A data silo is data trapped in an isolated system that other parts of the business cannot easily reach, which prevents a unified view and holds back analytics and AI. Governance is not only restriction: a catalog and self-service access let more people use data safely, bringing faster AI-driven insights, less duplicate data and stronger compliance. Interoperability means systems can exchange and use data through open standards, open formats and connectors. A proprietary format ties data to one engine and creates vendor lock-in, while open formats such as Apache Iceberg let different engines, such as SQL analytics or Apache Spark, work on the same data. Google Cloud positions itself as open, working with data across clouds and on premises.

examPoints: Data creates value through real-time insight, trends, strategic decisions and fueling AI, and AI results depend on the quality and organization of the underlying data.

Databases serve running applications, warehouses (BigQuery) serve analysis and reporting of mostly structured data, and lakes (often on Cloud Storage) keep raw data of all shapes for exploration and ML.

Remember the six supply chain stages in order (genesis, collection, processing, storage, analysis, activation), the first/second/third-party and structured/semi-structured/unstructured definitions, and that open formats and governance reduce silos and lock-in.

quiz.q: An analytics team uses one engine for SQL reports and another for large-scale data science jobs. Today each team keeps its own copy of the data in a different proprietary format, and switching tools means rewriting the data. What approach would best reduce copies and lock-in?
choices: Store the data in open formats such as Apache Iceberg so different engines can work on the same data
Move all of the data into a single proprietary format that only the newest engine can read and write
Keep each team's separate copy and add a nightly manual export between the two environments
Delete the older copy and require every team to use only SQL reports and no other tools
quiz.explain: Open formats are published specifications that many tools can use, so one copy can serve several engines and switching costs fall. Another proprietary format only repeats the lock-in. Manual exports are the symptom of missing interoperability, not the cure.

quiz.q: Every month-end, an online store's checkout becomes slow because finance runs reports over several years of sales on the same database that records customer orders. What is the best approach?
choices: Move the order-recording application into a data lake because lakes handle many small order updates faster
Ask finance to run its reports only during the day, because reporting and order updates never compete
Delete historical sales so the database stays small, even though trend analysis would be lost
Copy the data to a data warehouse such as BigQuery for analysis, and keep the database for recording orders
quiz.explain: Databases handle many small reads and writes, while warehouses are built for large analytical scans over history. Separating the two keeps customer-facing updates fast. A lake is not the right tool for transactional order recording, and deleting history gives up the trends that make data valuable.

days.recap: Data is valuable when it drives action: real-time insight, trends, decisions and AI. Databases run applications, warehouses analyze, lakes keep raw data. Know first/second/third-party and the three shapes, the six supply chain stages, and that governance plus open formats break silos and lock-in.

days.title: Choosing Google Cloud Data Storage and Database Services

concepts.heading: Relational and Non-Relational Databases
concepts.body: Relational databases organize data into tables of rows and columns with defined relationships and a fixed schema, and they are queried with SQL. Their key promise is the transaction: a group of changes either all happen or none do, and every reader afterwards sees the same result, called strong consistency. Google Cloud examples are Cloud SQL, AlloyDB and Spanner. Non-relational, or NoSQL, databases use other models such as documents, wide-column stores and key-value pairs. The schema is often flexible, and many designs scale out very widely for simple access patterns. Firestore and Bigtable are Google Cloud examples. Object storage is a third idea: data kept as whole objects, such as images or backups, inside buckets, retrieved by name and not queried with SQL. Cloud Storage is Google Cloud's object storage. A quick way to choose a family is to read the scenario for its signals. Money transfers and order records that must always be correct suggest relational. Millions of simple timestamped readings or changing document fields suggest NoSQL. Photos, video and PDFs fetched by name suggest object storage. Large analysis over history suggests a warehouse, not any of these.

concepts.heading: The Relational Services: Cloud SQL, AlloyDB, and Spanner
concepts.body: Google Cloud offers three relational choices, and the right one depends on scale and consistency needs. Cloud SQL runs MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server as a fully managed service: Google handles backups, patching, replication and failover, and the application keeps talking to the engine it already knows. It is ideal for regional applications of moderate size and for teams wanting the lowest effort move without rewriting. AlloyDB for PostgreSQL is a fully managed, PostgreSQL-compatible database built for demanding workloads that need higher performance, availability and scale, including mixed transactional and analytical use. A company that stays on PostgreSQL but has outgrown a general-purpose setup is the typical fit. Spanner is Google Cloud's globally distributed relational database, combining SQL and strong transactional consistency with horizontal scale and very high availability. A global retailer or payments company that needs many writers on several continents to see one correct answer, with no planned downtime, points to Spanner. Do not over-buy: the largest product for a small tool adds complexity, and a regional product for a global payment system risks the consistency needed.

concepts.heading: The NoSQL and Analytics Services: Bigtable, Firestore, and BigQuery
concepts.body: Bigtable is Google Cloud's wide-column NoSQL database. Rows are found by a single key, and it scales to billions of rows with high throughput and low latency. Typical uses are time-series data, Internet of Things data from sensors and meters, and large inputs for analytics or machine learning that need fast key-based reads and writes. Millions of small timestamped records looked up by device, with no joins, is the pattern. Firestore is a fully managed, serverless document database for mobile, web and server applications. Each record is a flexible JSON-like document, so records can have different fields without a schema change, and it offers built-in real-time synchronization and offline handling. A collaborative mobile app with offline editing fits. BigQuery is a different kind of service: a fully managed, serverless data warehouse for analysis. Analysts use SQL, and Google runs the infrastructure with no servers to size or tune, which suits years of history and large aggregations for business intelligence. Remember the split: Cloud SQL, AlloyDB, Spanner, Bigtable and Firestore serve applications with many small reads and writes, while BigQuery serves analysis.

concepts.heading: Cloud Storage Classes
concepts.body: Cloud Storage is object storage with effectively unlimited capacity and worldwide access. It offers storage classes that trade storage cost against access cost. Four are location-flexible: Standard for frequently accessed data, Nearline for data read about once a month or less, Coldline for data read about once a quarter or less, and Archive for data accessed less than once a year, kept for backup, regulatory or disaster-recovery reasons. A fifth class, Rapid, is a high-performance class available only in zonal buckets, placed in the same zone as compute for I/O-intensive work such as AI training, where faster data delivery keeps expensive accelerators busy. In the four classic classes data stays online and available in milliseconds, not hours. The colder the class, the lower the storage cost, but the higher the access cost, and colder classes also have a minimum storage duration and retrieval fees. So a rarely read archive is cheap in Archive, while a frequently read object in Archive can cost more than it saves. When access patterns are unpredictable, Autoclass manages classes automatically, moving objects that are not accessed to colder classes and returning accessed ones to Standard.

concepts.heading: Migrating and Modernizing Databases
concepts.body: Moving a database is not just copying files, because the source keeps changing while the copy runs and the business cannot stop. Database Migration Service moves data to Google Cloud with minimal downtime: it manages the networking, takes an initial snapshot, keeps replicating ongoing changes, and reports progress. When the migration completes, the destination becomes the primary database and the source can be shut down. It supports migrations into Cloud SQL and AlloyDB for PostgreSQL, so a self-managed MySQL database goes to Cloud SQL for MySQL. Landing on a managed service is the main modernization benefit. A self-managed database means the company runs servers, the operating system and maintenance itself. With a managed service such as Cloud SQL, AlloyDB or Spanner, Google operates the infrastructure and automates backups, patching, replication and failover. Staff time moves from maintenance to work that differentiates the business, capacity follows demand without a large hardware purchase, and availability features are built in. The customer still owns its data, schema and access decisions. Pick a service that supports the engine the application already uses so no rewrite is needed.

examPoints: Cloud SQL is the low-effort managed MySQL, PostgreSQL or SQL Server choice, AlloyDB is the high-performance PostgreSQL-compatible choice, and Spanner is the globally consistent, always-on relational choice.

Bigtable fits huge key-based time-series and IoT data, Firestore fits flexible documents with real-time sync for apps, Cloud Storage holds objects, and BigQuery is the serverless warehouse for analysis.

Choose a Cloud Storage class by access frequency (Standard, Nearline, Coldline, Archive; Rapid for zonal I/O-intensive work), use Autoclass for unpredictable patterns, and use Database Migration Service for minimal-downtime moves.

quiz.q: A commodities trading firm records millions of price ticks every second. Each tick is a small record identified by the instrument and the time, it is read back by key within milliseconds, and no joins between tables are needed. Which service fits best?
choices: Spanner, because it is the right choice whenever data arrives in very large volumes, whether or not it needs relational transactions
Bigtable, because it is a wide-column NoSQL database built for huge volumes of keyed time-series data with low latency
BigQuery, because it is built to serve low-latency single-record lookups for a live application at any volume of incoming ticks
Cloud Storage Archive, because tick history should be kept in the cheapest class at all times, whatever the access pattern or latency need
quiz.explain: Keyed, high-throughput time-series records read with low latency are the Bigtable pattern. Spanner is for relational data needing global strong consistency, which is not asked for here. BigQuery is for analysis over history, and Archive suits data read less than once a year, not data read in milliseconds.

quiz.q: A manufacturer runs its self-managed PostgreSQL order database in its own data center. It wants to move to Google Cloud, keep the same database engine so applications need no rewrite, and keep the system running during the move. Which approach fits?
choices: Export the database to files once a month and load them into Cloud Storage Nearline, then restore them when the old system is retired
Rewrite the application for Firestore so that it no longer depends on a relational engine, then cut over after the rewrite is finished
Use Database Migration Service to replicate the database into a managed PostgreSQL service such as Cloud SQL or AlloyDB
Shut down the system, copy the data by hand over a weekend, and accept an unplanned outage if anything goes wrong during the copy
quiz.explain: Database Migration Service takes a snapshot, keeps replicating ongoing changes and then promotes the destination, giving minimal downtime into a managed engine with the same compatibility. Loading files into a storage class does not create a running database, and a rewrite for Firestore contradicts the no-rewrite goal.

days.recap: Relational: Cloud SQL (managed, regional), AlloyDB (demanding PostgreSQL), Spanner (global, strongly consistent). NoSQL: Bigtable (keyed, huge scale), Firestore (documents, sync). Objects go to Cloud Storage classes by access frequency, analysis goes to BigQuery, and Database Migration Service moves databases with minimal downtime.

days.title: Analytics: BI, Streaming, Pub/Sub, Dataflow, and Apache Spark

concepts.heading: Business Intelligence with Looker
concepts.body: Business intelligence (BI) turns data into reports, dashboards and answers for decision makers. Two problems usually limit its value: only a few specialists can query the data, and different teams calculate the same metric differently. Looker is Google Cloud's BI platform. It offers self-service exploration and natural-language questions so business users can work with data without waiting for an analyst. It also uses a semantic layer, in which metrics are defined once and reused everywhere, so net sales means the same thing in every dashboard. This is democratizing data access with governance: more people use data, and they use the same trusted numbers. Looker connects to data sources such as BigQuery and presents the results as dashboards and reports. Example: a retailer's central warehouse is queried by a small analyst team while store managers wait days for answers and quote different revenue figures. Adding Looker lets managers explore data themselves while the shared metric definitions keep the figures consistent. Looker is the visualization and exploration layer, not the place where data is stored or processed.

concepts.heading: BigQuery for Analysis at Scale
concepts.body: BigQuery is Google Cloud's fully managed, serverless data warehouse. Serverless means Google runs and scales the infrastructure, so the company has no servers to size, patch or tune. Analysts use SQL (and Python) to ask questions of very large volumes of data, and Google describes it as handling terabytes in seconds and petabytes in minutes for business intelligence and ad hoc analysis. It can combine data from many sources, keep current and historical data together, and support continuous streaming ingestion so new records are available for analysis soon after they arrive. It also underpins Google Cloud's AI-ready data platform, because data analyzed or prepared in BigQuery can feed machine learning and AI workloads. When a scenario says years of history, large aggregations, analysts who know SQL and no desire to manage servers, think BigQuery. Do not use it as the operational database for an application that records many small updates, which is the job of databases such as Cloud SQL or Spanner. Example: a national retailer analyzing ten years of sales, loyalty and web-traffic history to find seasonal trends.

concepts.heading: The Business Value of Streaming Analytics
concepts.body: Batch analytics collects data over a period and processes it later, for example overnight. Its results describe the past. Streaming, or real-time, analytics processes each event as it arrives, so results describe the present. The business value is timeliness: when the value of an action falls quickly with time, waiting for a batch means missed opportunity or avoidable loss. Examples include stopping a fraudulent card payment before it completes instead of discovering it the next morning, rerouting a delivery around a delay, adjusting a price as demand changes, or letting an operations team watch orders and couriers on a live dashboard. Streaming does not replace historical analysis, because models and trends are still built on history, and it does not make risk disappear. It shortens the time between an event and a response. A common Google Cloud pattern follows the data supply chain: Pub/Sub collects events, Dataflow processes them, BigQuery stores and analyzes results, and Looker visualizes them. Each service has one clear job and the managed services scale without servers to run.

concepts.heading: Pub/Sub and Dataflow
concepts.body: Pub/Sub is an asynchronous, scalable messaging service. Producers of events are publishers that send messages to a topic without knowing who will read them. Consumers are subscribers that receive messages at their own pace. Because neither side waits for the other, one slow or offline consumer does not stop the senders. Typical uses are ingesting events from users, servers and Internet of Things devices, distributing events to many applications, and feeding stream-processing tools such as Dataflow. Example: millions of smart thermostats send readings, and alerting, billing and analytics systems each need them independently, which is a publish and subscribe pattern. Dataflow is Google Cloud's fully managed service for data pipelines, which move data from sources to destinations and transform it on the way. It uses one programming model, based on the open source Apache Beam project, for both batch and streaming data, and it adds and removes worker machines automatically as volume changes. Common uses are ETL (extract, transform, load) into a warehouse such as BigQuery, real-time analysis of streams and processing of sensor or log data. Pub/Sub carries messages; it does not run the computation.

concepts.heading: Managed Service for Apache Spark and Choosing a Pipeline Engine
concepts.body: Many companies already process data with open source tools such as Apache Spark and Hadoop. Managed Service for Apache Spark, the new name for Dataproc on Compute Engine in its cluster deployment, runs these tools on Google Cloud. Teams can move existing jobs without redevelopment, create clusters quickly and turn them off when finished so they do not pay for idle capacity. It integrates with BigQuery, Cloud Storage and Bigtable and reduces the administration of running clusters on premises. The choice between the two processing services follows where the team starts. Dataflow is best when building a new pipeline and wanting the least operations work, because it is fully managed and covers batch and streaming with automatic scaling. Managed Service for Apache Spark is best when a company already has Spark or Hadoop code or skills and wants to move without rewriting. Example: a bank with hundreds of existing Spark jobs chooses Managed Service for Apache Spark for a fast migration, while a media company designing a new clickstream pipeline chooses Dataflow.

examPoints: Looker is the BI platform with self-service exploration and a semantic layer that defines each metric once, while BigQuery is the serverless warehouse that stores and analyzes the data.
Streaming analytics is valuable when the worth of an action decays quickly; the standard pattern is Pub/Sub to collect, Dataflow to process, BigQuery to analyze and Looker to visualize.
Choose Dataflow for new batch or streaming pipelines with minimal operations, and Managed Service for Apache Spark to move existing Spark or Hadoop workloads without rewriting.

quiz.q: A hospital's bedside monitors continuously send events. The alerting system, the patient-records system and the analytics team each need their own copy of the events, and the monitors must keep sending even if one of those systems goes offline. Which service fits?
choices: Looker, because it presents the events to each team as dashboards and lets them share metric definitions
Managed Service for Apache Spark, because it processes the events in clusters that every team can then read from
Pub/Sub, because publishers send messages to a topic and each subscriber receives them independently at its own pace
Cloud Storage Archive, because the safest way to share events is to store them and read them once a year
quiz.explain: Pub/Sub decouples senders from receivers, so one offline consumer does not stop the monitors. Looker visualizes data but does not move events between systems. Spark clusters process data and do not provide messaging between independent consumers. Archive holds rarely read data and cannot deliver live events.

quiz.q: A marketing team of analysts who know SQL wants to explore several petabytes of campaign history, with no servers to size or manage. Which service is the best fit?
choices: Firestore, because it is a document database for serving mobile app data with real-time sync
BigQuery, because it is a serverless data warehouse where analysts query very large datasets with SQL
Cloud SQL, because it is a managed relational database designed for large analytical scans of history
Pub/Sub, because it stores campaign history permanently so analysts can query it directly
quiz.explain: Large history, SQL skills and no server management describe BigQuery. Firestore serves application data, Cloud SQL is an operational relational database for moderate-size regional applications, and Pub/Sub delivers messages rather than storing history for analysis.

days.recap: Looker gives self-service BI with metrics defined once, and BigQuery is the serverless warehouse behind it. Streaming analytics matters when action value decays fast: Pub/Sub collects, Dataflow processes, BigQuery analyzes, Looker visualizes. Use Managed Service for Apache Spark to move existing Spark or Hadoop jobs.

days.title: AI Fundamentals, Agentic AI, Data Quality, and Responsible AI

concepts.heading: AI, ML, Gen AI, Analytics, and BI
concepts.body: Four terms are often mixed up, so learn what each one produces. Artificial intelligence (AI) is the broad goal of software that performs tasks we associate with human intelligence. Machine learning (ML) is the part of AI in which a system learns patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules, and it usually outputs a prediction or a classification. Generative AI is ML that creates new content such as text, images or code. Data analytics is the wider practice of examining data to find insight, and business intelligence (BI) is the part of analytics that presents historical and current data in dashboards and reports so people can monitor the business and decide. A hospital director who opens a weekly dashboard of admissions and bed occupancy is using BI: the data is summarized, not predicted. If the same hospital scores each patient's chance of readmission, that is ML. If it asks a model to draft the discharge letter, that is gen AI. On the exam, match the verb in the scenario: show and report means BI, predict or classify means ML, create new content means gen AI.

concepts.heading: Agentic AI and AI Agents
concepts.body: Generative AI answers a prompt. Agentic AI goes further: an AI agent is given a goal, plans the steps needed, uses connected tools and business systems to act, and returns the result for a person to review. The difference is action. A chat assistant can explain how to rebook a flight, while an agent can check the traveller's calendar, search fares, propose an itinerary and, once approved, update the booking system. Agents are most useful where work is repetitive, spans several systems and follows a goal, such as support requests, sales research or reading scientific literature and proposing hypotheses for scientists to test. Because agents act, good practice matters: give them narrow permissions, require human approval for sensitive actions, ground them in the organization's own data so answers come from trusted repositories, and monitor results as the scope grows. Google Cloud offers Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform to build, deploy and manage agents, but at this level the idea matters more than the product: a goal, a plan, tools and human oversight.

concepts.heading: When ML Fits a Business Problem
concepts.body: ML is not always the answer, and the exam tests the judgment. ML fits when the pattern is too complex or changes too often for hand-written rules, when enough historical data exists, and when a probabilistic answer is acceptable. A card issuer maintaining thousands of fixed fraud rules is a classic case: fraudsters adapt, rules go stale, and a model trained on labelled past transactions can learn new patterns and reduce both missed fraud and wrongly blocked cards. Personalizing offers for millions of customers is another, because a model can score each customer automatically at a scale analysts cannot reach by hand. ML does not fit when the logic is known, exact and must be repeatable. A water bill that follows a published tariff table should be calculated with ordinary software, since ML would add uncertainty and cost without value. Unstructured data such as notes, photos and call recordings is a strength of modern AI, because it can turn them into information that can be analyzed alongside structured tables. Ask first whether rules could do the job exactly.

concepts.heading: Data Quality Dimensions
concepts.body: An AI model learns from its training data, so errors and gaps in the data are learned and reproduced in predictions. A first pilot that produces unreliable results often has a data problem, not a model problem. Data quality is described by dimensions, which are generally accepted ideas and not Google Cloud products. Completeness asks whether required information is present, so missing diagnosis codes break completeness. Uniqueness asks whether each real-world thing is recorded once, so a customer entered three times inflates the member count. Timeliness asks whether data is recent enough for the decision, so a nightly batch is too old for dispatch decisions made every minute. Validity asks whether values follow the required format and range, so a birth date typed as free text fails. Accuracy asks whether the value matches reality, and a colour listed as Teal is valid but not accurate if the product is red. Consistency asks whether the same fact agrees across systems, as when finance and sales report different revenue. Name the dimension from the symptom.

concepts.heading: Explainable and Responsible AI
concepts.body: Explainability means being able to show why a model produced a result, for example which inputs drove a loan decision. It matters because a declined applicant may ask for a reason, regulators may ask the lender to justify outcomes, and the lender needs to spot bias before it harms customers. Responsible AI is the broader set of practices for building and using AI safely and fairly: fairness testing, transparency and documentation, privacy protection, security, and human oversight. These are not only ethical extras. They help an organization meet regulatory and audit expectations, protect customer trust and avoid costly incidents. Consider a health insurer deciding whether to invest: bias testing and documentation lower legal and reputational risk, and human review keeps accountability with people for high-impact decisions. The exam usually frames this as a business benefit, so answers that tie responsible AI to trust, compliance and risk reduction beat answers that treat it as a cost with no return or as a purely technical setting.

examPoints: Show and report is BI, predict or classify is ML, create new content is gen AI, and an agent plans and acts toward a goal with tools and human oversight.
Use ML when rules cannot keep up and data exists; use ordinary software when the logic is known, exact and repeatable.
Name the data-quality dimension from the symptom (missing = completeness, duplicates = uniqueness, stale = timeliness, bad format = validity, wrong = accuracy, disagreeing systems = consistency).

quiz.q: A hotel chain's analysts want to know which of its 300 properties had the lowest occupancy last quarter. A manager also wants a tool that estimates which guests will probably cancel next month. Which pairing is correct?
choices: Occupancy by property is a business intelligence report, and the cancellation estimate is a predictive machine learning task
Occupancy by property needs generative AI, and the cancellation estimate is a business intelligence report
Both requests are generative AI because each one involves reading the hotel's historical booking data
Both requests are business intelligence because each one relies on data that is stored in tables
quiz.explain: Summarizing past results is BI, while estimating a future outcome per guest is ML prediction. Choice B reverses the two, and generative AI is about creating new content, which neither request asks for.

quiz.q: A distributor's customer table lists the same company as Acme Ltd, ACME Limited and Acme, so sales totals per customer are split across three rows. Which data-quality dimension is mainly violated?
choices: Timeliness, because the data was loaded too long ago to support today's decisions
Uniqueness, because one real customer is recorded several times and counted separately
Validity, because the company names do not follow a single required numeric format
Completeness, because some mandatory customer fields were left empty by the sales team
quiz.explain: One real-world entity appearing as several records is a uniqueness problem. Choice C is tempting because the spellings differ, but validity concerns values that break a defined format or range, not duplicate entities.

days.recap: BI reports on the past, ML predicts, gen AI creates and agents plan and act with tools under human oversight. Use ML when rules cannot keep up, judge data by completeness, uniqueness, timeliness, validity, accuracy and consistency, and treat explainable, responsible AI as a way to earn trust and meet audits.

days.title: Choosing Google Cloud AI Solutions

concepts.heading: Five Factors for Choosing an AI Approach
concepts.body: When a leader must get an AI capability, five factors guide the choice. Speed: how soon the business needs it. Development effort: how much building, data preparation and maintenance the team must carry. Differentiation: whether the capability is a competitive edge or a commodity. Technical expertise: whether people exist who can build and run models. Choice and flexibility: whether the business can change models or tools later. On Google Cloud the options form a spectrum. At one end are ready-made, pre-trained APIs, which are fastest and need the least expertise. In the middle are foundation models such as Gemini, steered with prompts. Further along are AutoML and custom training on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, which cost more data, time and skill but allow results shaped by your own data. An insurer that must add call transcription before its busy season in six weeks, with no ML staff, should start at the pre-trained end. A lender with fifteen years of proprietary repayment history and time to invest may build further along. Common task plus deadline favors buying; a unique asset favors building.

concepts.heading: Pre-Trained APIs
concepts.body: Google Cloud offers pre-trained AI services that a company calls through an API without training anything. Cloud Vision API analyzes images to detect text, labels and explicit content. Cloud Translation translates text and documents between many languages. Speech-to-Text converts audio to text, and Text-to-Speech works in the other direction. These services are trained by Google on broad data and are available to every customer, so they are quick, need little expertise and cost little effort to adopt. Their limit is that they know general things. A used-car marketplace can use Vision to read licence plates in seller photos; a furniture seller can translate manuals for each shopper. But a food manufacturer whose line has plant-specific packaging faults will find that a general image service labels common objects and misses its own defects. That is the signal to move toward a model trained on its own labelled photos. Also beware over-building: an airline that spent nine months creating a custom translation model for a commodity task would have been better served by Cloud Translation.

concepts.heading: Foundation Models, Agent Platform, Model Garden, and Agent Studio
concepts.body: Foundation models such as Gemini are trained broadly and can be steered by prompts, which is often the quickest route to a new feature because it needs no training data or model-building skills. Gemini is multimodal, so one model can read a guest's typed question and a photo together and answer in text. Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI) is Google Cloud's managed platform to find and use models, build and deploy agents and apps, and train and manage custom ML models across their lifecycle. Within it, Model Garden is the place to discover and use Google, partner and open models, which gives choice and flexibility: a media group worried about depending on one supplier can try and switch among models. Agent Studio is a low-code environment for designing and prototyping with models and agents, so a product manager can test different instructions and share the design without writing code. Think of Agent Platform as the whole workshop, Model Garden as the catalog and Agent Studio as the sketchpad.

concepts.heading: AutoML, Custom Training, and BigQuery ML
concepts.body: When a pre-trained service is not enough, Google Cloud gives several ways to build a model from your own data. AutoML on Agent Platform is codeless: you provide a managed, labelled dataset such as tabular records or images, and the service chooses and trains a model for a predefined objective like classification or regression. Custom training allows any objective and full control, but needs programmers and data-science expertise and more effort. A mail-order retailer predicting churn from purchase tables with no coders fits AutoML. A team with a unique objective fits custom training. BigQuery ML lets analysts create and run models with standard SQL directly where the data already sits in BigQuery. Its business benefits are that analysts use skills they already have and large datasets need not be moved or reformatted for separate ML tools. A grocery chain with SQL-fluent analysts and data in BigQuery would forecast demand there. BigQuery ML can also call a Gemini model or a Cloud AI API over text stored in a table.

concepts.heading: AI Hypercomputer and Matching Needs to Solutions
concepts.body: AI Hypercomputer is Google Cloud's integrated supercomputing architecture for AI workloads, combining purpose-built hardware such as TPUs and GPUs with software and consumption options. It is aimed at organizations that train and serve large models themselves and need that scale, such as a media company whose on-premises servers cannot keep up with training. It is not the starting point for ordinary business tasks. A regional clinic that wants dictation turned into text should call a pre-trained speech API first, not buy a cluster of accelerators. A useful way to finish this topic is to practise sorting a bundle of requests. Weekly store demand forecast from warehouse tables built by SQL analysts points to BigQuery ML. Captions for product photos point to a pre-trained vision service or Gemini. A truly unique prediction objective with its own data points to custom training on Agent Platform. A contact centre needing transcripts and short summaries can chain Speech-to-Text and a Gemini model. Choose the simplest tool that meets the need.

examPoints: Common task, tight deadline and no ML staff point to a pre-trained API; proprietary data and a need to stand out point to AutoML or custom training.
Agent Platform is the managed workshop, Model Garden is the catalog of Google, partner and open models, and Agent Studio is the low-code place to prototype.
BigQuery ML builds models with SQL where data already lives, and AI Hypercomputer is for organizations that train and serve large models themselves.

quiz.q: A tourism board wants its booking site to speak twelve languages within one month. Its team has no ML engineers and the translation quality of a standard service is acceptable. What should it do?
choices: Hire a research team to design a new translation model architecture for the board's destinations
Collect a large labelled corpus and train a custom translation model on Agent Platform
Use Cloud Translation through its API, which needs little effort or expertise and fits the deadline
Build an AI Hypercomputer cluster first so the board can later train language models on its own
quiz.explain: Translation is a commodity task, and a pre-trained API meets the deadline and skill limits. Choice B is tempting because it uses Google Cloud's training tools, but it adds data collection and expertise the board does not need.

quiz.q: A bank's marketing analysts know SQL, keep all customer data in BigQuery, and want to predict which customers will open a new savings account. Which choice reflects the main benefit of the approach they should use?
choices: They can build and run the model with SQL where the data already sits, without exporting large datasets to other tools
They can avoid labelling any data because the model teaches itself the customers' preferences
They gain access to purpose-built TPU clusters that the bank would otherwise have to buy itself
They can publish the model as a public API that other banks can call for a usage fee
quiz.explain: BigQuery ML brings model building to SQL users and keeps the data in place. Choice B is wrong because predicting an outcome from past examples needs labelled history, which the bank has in its records.

days.recap: Weigh speed, effort, differentiation, expertise and flexibility. Pre-trained APIs suit common tasks fast, Gemini is steered by prompts, Agent Platform with Model Garden and Agent Studio covers models and agents, AutoML and custom training build from your data, BigQuery ML uses SQL, and AI Hypercomputer serves large-scale training.

days.title: Migration Strategies and Core Compute Concepts

concepts.heading: Migration Planning Terms: Workloads, Discovery, and Assessment
concepts.body: A workload is an application or service together with the resources and data it needs to run. A hospital group planning its move lists the patient-scheduling system, the billing database and the imaging archive: each is a workload, and each may get a different treatment. Migration starts with discovery and assessment. Discovery inventories the workloads and their dependencies, meaning which systems talk to which, who owns them and how much they are used. Assessment evaluates how each should be migrated and in what order. A manufacturer with 400 applications and no complete list cannot plan reliably until this is done, because moving a system without knowing what depends on it breaks things nobody expected. A CFO asking what makes a migration plan reliable should therefore expect an inventory with owners, dependencies and current usage. This is why assessment comes before moving anything. It also shows which applications nobody uses any more, and those save the most money because they need no migration at all.

concepts.heading: Migration Strategies from Retain to Reimagine
concepts.body: Each workload gets one strategy. Retain: keep it where it is for now, often because of a regulatory or hardware constraint, and revisit later. Retire: decommission it, for example a reporting tool nobody has opened in two years, so no effort or money is spent on it. Rehost, also called lift and shift: move it as it is to virtual machines, which is fastest with the fewest changes but does not yet use cloud-native features. Replatform: make one targeted improvement, such as moving a self-managed database to a managed one, while the application code stays the same. Refactor: modify the code and architecture to take advantage of cloud capabilities, for example splitting a monolith. Reimagine: use cloud and AI to rethink how the process or business works, such as an insurer redesigning claims around automation. Short deadline and a vendor package that cannot be changed means rehost; slow, hard-to-change monolith means refactor. Rehosting is a good first step, but the agility and cost gains arrive only as workloads later adopt managed or autoscaling features.

concepts.heading: Virtual Machines and Containers
concepts.body: A virtual machine (VM) emulates a whole computer, including its own operating system, on shared physical hardware. Customers choose the operating system, size and installed software, and they manage everything inside the VM. This control suits applications that expect a particular environment. A container packages an application with its dependencies and shares the host operating system's kernel, so it is lighter than a VM and starts quickly. Its main business value is consistency: a team builds the application once and runs it the same way on a laptop, in testing and in production. Containers also suit microservices, an architecture in which an application is split into small, independently deployable services connected by APIs. An online retailer whose single large application handles search, cart and payments can gain from microservices: a defect in recommendations no longer takes down checkout, each service is released and scaled on its own, and teams work independently. The cost is more components to run, which is why platforms that orchestrate containers become important.

concepts.heading: Serverless, Managed Services, and Spot VMs
concepts.body: Serverless computing means the provider allocates and scales resources on demand and bills for actual use, so developers deploy code without provisioning or managing servers. It suits unpredictable or bursty work, such as an app that processes photo uploads in a few minutes of activity and then sits idle for hours. The trade-off is less control over the underlying environment than VMs offer. Managed services extend the idea to infrastructure: Google operates the underlying platform and handles tasks such as patching and backups, which frees a small IT team that spends its week on routine database upkeep. Spot VMs are spare Compute Engine capacity sold at a much lower cost, but Google can reclaim them, so the work must tolerate interruption. A nightly genome-processing batch that restarts from checkpoints and finishes within hours is a good fit, while a customer-facing checkout system is not. Move along the responsibility spectrum, VMs then containers then serverless, as the team wants Google to handle more operations.

concepts.heading: Kubernetes, Autoscaling, and Load Balancing
concepts.body: Once dozens of services are containers, operators need help keeping the right number of copies running, restarting failed ones and rolling out updates. Kubernetes is an open source system that orchestrates the deployment, scaling and management of containers. Autoscaling adds resources when demand rises and removes them when it drops. A ticket seller whose traffic jumps tenfold within minutes at sales opening used to buy hardware for the peak and watch it sit idle; with autoscaling, cost follows actual use. A load balancer distributes incoming requests across healthy servers, often spread over several zones, so visitors do not hit a failing server and capacity is used evenly. Together they deliver availability and cost efficiency, two benefits the exam repeats. Do not confuse them: autoscaling changes how many servers exist, load balancing decides which server receives each request, and Kubernetes coordinates the containers that run on those servers. In the cloud model, these capabilities arrive as managed services instead of equipment the company must buy.

examPoints: Discovery and assessment inventory workloads and dependencies before any move; each workload then gets retain, retire, rehost, replatform, refactor or reimagine.
VMs give OS control, containers give consistent packaging, and serverless gives the provider most operations at the price of less control.
Spot VMs are cheap but reclaimable and suit interruption-tolerant batch work; autoscaling matches capacity to demand and load balancing spreads requests over healthy servers.

quiz.q: A broadcaster must vacate its data center in ten weeks. Its scheduling application runs on VMs, works well, and the vendor does not support changes to the code. Which strategy fits and what is its limitation?
choices: Refactor, because it makes the application take full advantage of cloud-native services right away
Reimagine, because it rethinks the broadcasting process and delivers the fastest possible exit
Retire, because decommissioning the system is the only way to meet an exit date this close
Rehost, because it moves the application with the fewest changes, but cloud-native features are not yet used
quiz.explain: Rehost is fastest and keeps the vendor-supported code intact, while the limitation is that cloud-native benefits come later. Choice A is tempting for its benefits, but a refactor takes far longer than ten weeks and the vendor forbids code changes.

quiz.q: A game studio launches a new title and expects player traffic to swing sharply between peak evenings and quiet mornings. Which combination best protects availability and controls cost?
choices: Autoscaling to adjust capacity to demand, and load balancing to spread requests across healthy servers
A fixed fleet sized for the peak, and a single large server in one zone to keep operations simple
Autoscaling alone, with every request sent to the same server so session data stays in one place
Load balancing alone, with a fleet sized once at launch and left unchanged during later demand swings
quiz.explain: Autoscaling matches capacity to demand and load balancing routes requests to healthy servers, giving availability and efficiency. Choice B is tempting for its simplicity but pays for idle peak capacity and creates a single point of failure.
